question: The Diwani (revenue rights) of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa was granted to Robert Clive in 1765 by the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II through which treaty?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Treaty of Allahabad.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Treaty of Allahabad (1765) followed the Battle of Buxar (1764) and was signed between Robert Clive and the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II (इलाहाबाद की संधि — क्लाइव को बंगाल, बिहार और उड़ीसा की दीवानी मिली)

 

• By this treaty the East India Company became the legal Diwan of the three provinces, collecting land revenue on behalf of the emperor in return for an annual tribute of Rs 26 lakh.

 

• Shuja-ud-daula, the Nawab of Awadh, who had fought at Buxar, was allowed to keep Awadh after paying an indemnity, while Kara and Allahabad were handed to the emperor.

 

• The grant converted the Company from a trading body into a territorial power with a secure revenue base in eastern India.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Clive was Governor of Bengal twice, in 1757-60 and again from 1765 to 1767, and he reached India for the second term in 1765.

 

• The Diwani grant set up the system known as Dual Government, in which the Company held revenue powers while the Nawab retained criminal justice.

 

• The Battle of Buxar was fought on 22 October 1764 between Hector Munro's forces and the combined armies of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-daula and Shah Alam II.

 

• Clive had earlier become the first Governor of Fort William after the Battle of Plassey in 1757.

 

NOTE

 

• Treaty of Alinagar (Option 1): The Treaty of Alinagar (February 1757) was concluded between Siraj-ud-daula and the Company after Calcutta was recaptured, restoring the Company's trading privileges; it has no link with the Diwani grant, which came eight years later.

 

• Treaty of Bassein (Option 3): The Treaty of Bassein (1802) was signed between the Peshwa Baji Rao II and the British under Wellesley, making the Peshwa accept the Subsidiary Alliance; it belongs to Maratha affairs, not Bengal revenue.

 

• Treaty of Salbai (Option 4): The Treaty of Salbai (1782) ended the First Anglo-Maratha War during Warren Hastings's period; it was signed with the Marathas and has nothing to do with the Mughal emperor or the Diwani of Bengal.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Dual Government in Bengal.

1. It was introduced by Robert Clive in 1765.

2. Under it, the Nizamat covered revenue collection and civil justice, while the Diwani covered police and criminal justice.

3. It was abolished by Warren Hastings.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 3 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: after obtaining the Diwani in 1765, Robert Clive split Bengal's administration between the Company and the Nawab, a scheme called Dual Government (बंगाल में द्वैध शासन — क्लाइव, 1765)

 

• Statement 2 is wrong because the functions are reversed: the Diwani (held by the Company) meant revenue collection and civil justice, whereas the Nizamat (left with the Nawab) meant police and criminal justice.

 

• Statement 3 is correct: under the Regulating Act period, Warren Hastings ended the arrangement in 1772 and the Company began to act as Diwan itself, collecting revenue through its own agents.

 

• The system gave the Company power without responsibility and the Nawab responsibility without power, and it coincided with the terrible Bengal famine of 1770.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Company's deputy Diwans were Muhammad Reza Khan (Bengal) and Raja Shitab Roy (Bihar) during the dual system.

 

• Hastings shifted the treasury from Murshidabad to Calcutta and made Calcutta the capital of Bengal in 1772.

 

• The Regulating Act of 1773 later made Hastings the first Governor-General of Bengal.

 

• The Bengal famine of 1769-70 is reported to have killed roughly one-third of the population of the province.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 2 only (Option 2): The combination 1 and 2 only wrongly accepts the reversed definition in statement 2, since revenue and civil justice were the Diwani functions, not the Nizamat; it also leaves out the correct role of Warren Hastings in ending the system.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 3): The combination 2 and 3 only accepts the swapped definition in statement 2 while rejecting statement 1, yet Clive is firmly credited with starting the system in 1765 after the Treaty of Allahabad.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): The combination 1, 2 and 3 would be right only if the Nizamat and Diwani descriptions were correct; because statement 2 swaps police and criminal justice with revenue and civil justice, including it makes the choice wrong.

question: Which Company official committed suicide in 1774 after being censured by the British Parliament on charges of corruption?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Robert Clive.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Robert Clive, the victor of Plassey, took his own life in November 1774 after Parliament censured his acquisition of wealth in Bengal (रॉबर्ट क्लाइव — भ्रष्टाचार के आरोप के बाद 1774 में आत्महत्या)

 

• His fortune, including the jagir received from Mir Jafar after Plassey, drew an inquiry by a parliamentary committee in 1772-73, which found his conduct improper though it also noted his great services.

 

• Clive's second Governorship (1765-67) was devoted to curbing private trade and the 'double batta' mutiny of European officers, which made him many enemies in the Company.

 

• He is remembered as the founder of British power in Bengal, having served as first Governor of Fort William after Plassey (1757).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Clive was made Baron Clive of Plassey in the Irish peerage, and he is often called Clive of India.

 

• His Diwani acquisition of 1765 rested on the Treaty of Allahabad with Shah Alam II.

 

• Warren Hastings was impeached, not driven to suicide; his trial ended in acquittal in 1795.

 

• The Regulating Act of 1773 was passed partly because of the Company's financial and moral scandals of the Clive era.

 

NOTE

 

• Warren Hastings (Option 1): Warren Hastings faced impeachment proceedings in the House of Lords after returning to England in 1785, but he was acquitted in 1795 and lived on until 1818, so he did not die by suicide.

 

• Lord Cornwallis (Option 3): Lord Cornwallis died of fever at Ghazipur in October 1805 during his second term as Governor-General, a natural death far from any parliamentary censure for corruption.

 

• Lord Wellesley (Option 4): Lord Wellesley was criticised by the Directors for costly wars and recalled in 1805, but he lived until 1842 and faced no censure that ended in suicide.

question: Who became the first Governor-General of Bengal under the Regulating Act of 1773?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Warren Hastings.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Regulating Act of 1773 made the Governor of Bengal the Governor-General of Bengal, and Warren Hastings became its first holder, serving until 1785 (वारेन हेस्टिंग्स — बंगाल का प्रथम गवर्नर-जनरल)

 

• He was also the last Governor of Bengal, since he held the Governor's post from 1772 before being elevated to the new Governor-General's office.

 

• The Act gave him a council of four members and a casting vote, and it subordinated the Bombay and Madras Presidencies to Bengal in matters of war and peace.

 

• His term saw the abolition of Dual Government, judicial reorganisation, the First Anglo-Maratha War and the Second Anglo-Mysore War.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The same Act established a Supreme Court at Calcutta in 1774 with Elijah Impey as the first Chief Justice.

 

• The first Governor-General of India, as opposed to Bengal, was William Bentinck under the Charter Act of 1833.

 

• Hastings was the founder of the Calcutta Madrasa (1781) in a bid to win Muslim support.

 

• Pitt's India Act of 1784 later curtailed the powers of the Governor-General by creating the Board of Control.

 

NOTE

 

• Robert Clive (Option 1): Robert Clive's governorship ended in 1767, years before the 1773 Act created the post of Governor-General; he held the title Governor of Bengal and never held the new office.

 

• Lord Cornwallis (Option 2): Lord Cornwallis became Governor-General only in 1786, after the Pitt's India Act of 1784 had strengthened the office, and he is better known for the Permanent Settlement of 1793.

 

• William Bentinck (Option 3): William Bentinck served as Governor-General of Bengal from 1828 and then, from 1833, as the first Governor-General of India, but that is a much later office under the Charter Act of 1833.

question: The First Anglo-Maratha War (1775-1782) during the tenure of Warren Hastings ended with the signing of which treaty?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Treaty of Salbai.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Treaty of Salbai (1782) closed the First Anglo-Maratha War between the Company and the Marathas, bringing a period of peace for about twenty years (सालबाई की संधि — प्रथम आंग्ल-मराठा युद्ध का अंत)

 

• The war had begun over the British support to Raghunath Rao (Raghoba) in the Peshwa succession dispute, and it included the humiliating British surrender at Wadgaon in 1779.

 

• Mahadji Scindia mediated the settlement, and the British recognised the young Peshwa Madhav Rao II while Raghoba received a pension.

 

• In the same period Hastings handled the Second Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84), which ended with the Treaty of Mangalore (1784).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Treaty of Purandar (1776) was an earlier agreement that was later repudiated.

 

• The Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05) occurred under Wellesley and the Third (1817-18) under Lord Hastings.

 

• The Salbai settlement gave the Company Salsette and some adjoining islands near Bombay.

 

• Warren Hastings's policy of building buffer states is sometimes labelled the Ring Fence policy.

 

NOTE

 

• Treaty of Mangalore (Option 1): The Treaty of Mangalore (1784) ended the Second Anglo-Mysore War between Tipu Sultan and the Company, so it concerns Mysore and not the Marathas, although it was concluded in the same Hastings period.

 

• Treaty of Bassein (Option 2): The Treaty of Bassein (1802) with Peshwa Baji Rao II came during Wellesley's time and led to the Second Anglo-Maratha War; it is not the settlement of the 1775-82 conflict.

 

• Treaty of Amritsar (Option 4): The Treaty of Amritsar (1809) was signed by Charles Metcalfe on behalf of Lord Minto I with Maharaja Ranjit Singh of Punjab and is unrelated to the Maratha wars.

question:
Consider the following statements about the judicial reforms of Warren Hastings.

1. Each district was given a Diwani Adalat under the Collector for civil cases.

2. The Supreme Court at Calcutta was established in 1774 with Elijah Impey as its first Chief Justice.

3. The Sadar Diwani Adalat was set up at Bombay as the highest court of appeal.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: Hastings set up a Diwani Adalat in every district under the Collector for civil disputes and a Faujdari Adalat under an Indian officer for criminal cases (हेस्टिंग्स के न्यायिक सुधार — जिला दीवानी और फौजदारी अदालतें)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: the Regulating Act of 1773 provided the Supreme Court at Calcutta, which began in 1774 with Elijah Impey as the first Chief Justice.

 

• Statement 3 is wrong because the Sadar Diwani Adalat and Sadar Nizamat Adalat were the appellate courts at Calcutta, not at Bombay.

 

• Disputes on inheritance, marriage, caste and succession were to be decided under Hindu law for Hindus and Muslim law for Muslims.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Cornwallis Code (1793) later separated revenue from judicial functions and appointed Indian munsiffs at the lowest civil courts.

 

• Impey's court clashed with the Governor-General's council, and the Cossijurah case showed the conflict of jurisdictions.

 

• Hastings also compiled a Code of Gentoo Laws (1776) with the help of Pandits.

 

• The Regulating Act's Supreme Court applied English law and served the English residents of Calcutta.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 2): Choosing 1 and 3 only wrongly counts the Bombay claim; the highest civil appeal court, the Sadar Diwani Adalat, sat at Calcutta, and the pair also drops the correct Supreme Court statement.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 3): Selecting 2 and 3 only rejects the true district court arrangement under the Collector while accepting the false Bombay location for the Sadar Diwani Adalat, which functioned in Calcutta.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): All three statements cannot hold because the claim that the Sadar Diwani Adalat sat at Bombay is incorrect; the court of civil appeal was located in Calcutta under the Governor-General and council.

question: The Asiatic Society of Bengal, established in 1784, was founded with the support of Warren Hastings by
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sir William Jones.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Asiatic Society of Bengal was founded in Calcutta in 1784 by Sir William Jones, a judge of the Supreme Court and a great orientalist, with Hastings's encouragement (एशियाटिक सोसाइटी ऑफ बंगाल — विलियम जोन्स, 1784)

 

• It aimed at the study of Indian history, languages, science and literature, and its journal Asiatick Researches carried the findings to Europe.

 

• The patronage of Hastings to orientalism was part of his policy of ruling Indians through their own laws and traditions.

 

• Jones's discovery of the kinship between Sanskrit and European languages laid the base of comparative philology.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Charles Wilkins, a colleague of Hastings, made the first English translation of the Bhagavad Gita in 1785.

 

• James Hicky started the Bengal Gazette in 1780, the first newspaper in India.

 

• Jonathan Duncan founded the Sanskrit College at Benaras in 1791 during Cornwallis's period.

 

• H. T. Colebrooke and Wilkins were other early members of the Society.

 

NOTE

 

• Charles Wilkins (Option 1): Charles Wilkins is known for translating the Bhagavad Gita into English in 1785 with the encouragement of Warren Hastings; he assisted the orientalist project but was not the founder of the Society.

 

• James Augustus Hicky (Option 2): James Augustus Hicky launched Hicky's Bengal Gazette in 1780, the first newspaper in India, and has no role in founding a learned society, which was the work of a judge.

 

• Jonathan Duncan (Option 4): Jonathan Duncan, the Resident at Benaras, established the Sanskrit College there in 1791 under Cornwallis; this was a later institution of Sanskrit learning, not the 1784 Society.

question: Which Governor-General was impeached in the British Parliament after returning to England, though he was acquitted in 1795?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Warren Hastings.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Warren Hastings was the Governor-General who faced impeachment; proceedings began in 1787 after his return and he was finally acquitted in 1795 (वारेन हेस्टिंग्स — महाभियोग, 1795 में बरी)

 

• The prosecution was led by Edmund Burke with Fox and Sheridan, and it accused him of corruption and cruelty, including actions against Raja Chait Singh of Benaras and the Begums of Awadh.

 

• The trial dragged for nearly eight years and exhausted his fortune, although the Company later gave him a pension.

 

• He is the only Governor-General to have been impeached, which makes the fact a frequent exam question.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Hastings is credited with the Rohilla War (1774) and the Chait Singh affair of 1781.

 

• He was succeeded by Cornwallis in 1786 after a brief period under John Macpherson.

 

• Hastings's rule also included the Bengal Gazette, the Asiatic Society and the Calcutta Madrasa.

 

• Pitt's India Act (1784) had reduced the autonomy of the Governor-General during his final years.

 

NOTE

 

• Lord Cornwallis (Option 1): Lord Cornwallis was never impeached; he earned praise for the Permanent Settlement and the Third Mysore War, and he returned to India as Governor-General in 1805 only to die soon after.

 

• Lord Wellesley (Option 2): Lord Wellesley was strongly criticised for his expensive wars and a motion against him was raised in Parliament, but it did not lead to a trial and acquittal like the one of 1795.

 

• Lord Dalhousie (Option 3): Lord Dalhousie left India in 1856 in poor health and was never impeached; his annexations were criticised, yet the proceedings ending in 1795 predate his career by more than half a century.

question:
Consider the following statements about the administrative reforms of Lord Cornwallis.

1. The Cornwallis Code of 1793 was prepared with the help of George Barlow.

2. Each district was divided into thanas headed by an Indian official called a Daroga.

3. Indians were appointed as judges of the highest civil courts at Calcutta.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: the Cornwallis Code (1793) was framed with his colleague George Barlow and separated revenue administration from the administration of justice (कॉर्नवालिस कोड 1793 — पुलिस और न्यायिक सुधार)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: the police were reorganised by dividing each district into thanas (police circles), each under a Daroga, with the District Judge controlling the police.

 

• Statement 3 is wrong because Indians were appointed only to the lowest rung of the judiciary as Munsifs; the higher posts were reserved for Europeans.

 

• Cornwallis excluded Indians from higher offices, a policy that earned him the label of the founder of a service that was closed to Indians.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Cornwallis is called the Father of Civil Services in India for giving the service high salaries and ending private trade by officials.

 

• The Permanent Settlement of Bengal (1793) first started as a ten-year arrangement and was later made permanent.

 

• Satyendranath Tagore was the first Indian to enter the ICS, in 1863.

 

• The District Collector combined revenue powers with magistracy after later reforms.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 2): Opting for 1 and 3 only credits Indians with high judicial posts, which did not happen under Cornwallis, and it ignores the Daroga-led thana system that formed the police reform of his period.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 3): Going with 2 and 3 only drops the correct Barlow-assisted Code from consideration and wrongly accepts that Indians sat in the highest courts, when only Munsif posts at the base were open to them.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Accepting all three statements is incorrect because statement 3 is false; the upper judiciary and senior services stayed European, and only subordinate munsiffs and darogas were drawn from Indians.

question:
Assertion (A): Lord Cornwallis is regarded as the Father of Civil Services in India.

Reason (R): He gave the Company's servants high fixed salaries and ended their private trading, making the service honest and efficient.
option_1: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_2: A is true but R is false
option_3: A is false but R is true
option_4: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Assertion A is true: Cornwallis (Governor-General 1786-93) is called the Father of Civil Services in India because he organised the Company's covenanted service (कॉर्नवालिस — भारतीय सिविल सेवा के जनक)

 

• Reason R is also true: he raised the salaries of the Company's covenanted servants and banned private trade and acceptance of gifts, which reduced corruption.

 

• R correctly explains A, since the reform of pay and conduct created a disciplined, professional bureaucracy that became the base of the later ICS.

 

• The reform was racially exclusive; Indians were kept out of positions above a modest level for decades.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Indian Civil Service later acquired its name and competitive entry through the Charter Act of 1853 and the Macaulay Committee.

 

• Satyendranath Tagore, elder brother of Rabindranath, cleared the ICS examination in 1863.

 

• Written ICS examinations began in India in 1922, under Lord Reading.

 

• Lytton cut the maximum age for the ICS exam from 21 to 19 in 1876.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 1): The second option accepts both statements but denies the causal link; yet pay and the ban on private trade are exactly the measures that earned him the title of founder of the civil services.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 2): The third option calls the Reason false, but the high pay and prohibition on private trade for Company servants were indeed major elements of Cornwallis's reorganisation of the service.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 3): The fourth option calls the Assertion false, but the description of Cornwallis as the Father of Civil Services is standard in textbooks and is firmly stated in standard notes.

question: The Third Anglo-Mysore War (1790-1792), in which Lord Cornwallis personally led British forces, was fought against
solution_text:
The correct answer is Tipu Sultan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Third Anglo-Mysore War was fought against Tipu Sultan, who had attacked Travancore, an ally of the British, in 1789 (तृतीय आंग्ल-मैसूर युद्ध — टीपू सुल्तान बनाम कॉर्नवालिस)

 

• Cornwallis allied with the Marathas and the Nizam, besieged Srirangapatna and forced Tipu to sign the Treaty of Srirangapatam (1792).

 

• By the treaty Tipu surrendered nearly half of his kingdom and paid a heavy indemnity, and two of his sons were held as hostages.

 

• The territories ceded included Malabar, Dindigul and Baramahal, which strengthened British hold on southern India.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Haider Ali fought the First (1767-69) and Second (1780-84) Anglo-Mysore Wars, dying in 1782.

 

• The Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799) ended with Tipu's death at Srirangapatna under Wellesley.

 

• The Second Mysore War ended with the Treaty of Mangalore (1784) during Hastings's tenure.

 

• Tipu's name is linked to the 'tree of liberty' planted at Srirangapatna and rocket warfare.

 

NOTE

 

• Haider Ali (Option 1): Haider Ali was Tipu's father; he commanded Mysore in the First and Second Anglo-Mysore Wars and died in 1782, so he could not have been the opponent in the war of 1790-92.

 

• Mahadji Scindia (Option 3): Mahadji Scindia was a Maratha chief who mediated the Treaty of Salbai in 1782 and died in 1794; in 1790 the Marathas stood with the British against Mysore rather than against them.

 

• Nana Phadnavis (Option 4): Nana Phadnavis was the chief minister of the Peshwa at Poona and joined the British side in the Third Mysore War, so he was an ally and not the target of Cornwallis.

question: Which Governor-General formulated the Subsidiary Alliance system, with the Nizam of Hyderabad becoming the first ruler to accept it in 1798?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lord Wellesley.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Lord Wellesley (1798-1805) reversed the non-intervention policy of his predecessors and perfected the Subsidiary Alliance as his master plan (वेलेजली — सहायक संधि प्रणाली, 1798)

 

• The Nizam of Hyderabad was the first to accept it in 1798, followed by Mysore (1799), Tanjore (1799), Awadh (1801), the Peshwa (1802) and the Bhonsle and Scindia (1803).

 

• The ruler had to station a British army at his own cost and accept a British Resident, and could not enter alliances or employ other Europeans without permission.

 

• The alliance gradually drained the allied states of independence and revenue while expanding the Company's control.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Wellesley called himself the Bengal Tiger.

 

• He captured Delhi in 1803 and placed the Mughal emperor on a pension.

 

• He set up Fort William College (1800) at Calcutta to train civil servants.

 

• Dalhousie later used the Doctrine of Lapse as another instrument of annexation.

 

• The Subsidiary Alliance bound the ruler to pay for the British force, usually by ceding territory, which drained his treasury.

 

NOTE

 

• Lord Cornwallis (Option 1): Lord Cornwallis followed a policy of non-intervention and is known for the Permanent Settlement and the Cornwallis Code; he fought Tipu but did not construct a system of subsidiary treaties.

 

• Lord Dalhousie (Option 2): Lord Dalhousie came half a century later and annexed states through the Doctrine of Lapse; the subsidiary scheme was already in decline by then and was not his device.

 

• Lord Hastings (Option 3): Lord Hastings (1813-23) continued the policy of paramountcy and destroyed the Pindaris and the Peshwa power, but the Subsidiary Alliance originated earlier with Wellesley.

question: Which of the following is NOT associated with the tenure of Lord Wellesley?
option_3: Censorship of the Press Act of 1799
option_4: Acceptance of the Subsidiary Alliance by the Peshwa
solution_text:
The correct answer is Introduction of the Permanent Settlement.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Permanent Settlement was introduced in 1793 by Lord Cornwallis, not by Wellesley, who came to office only in 1798 (स्थायी बंदोबस्त — कॉर्नवालिस, 1793, वेलेजली नहीं)

 

• Fort William College was founded by Wellesley in 1800 at Calcutta to train young Company officials in Indian languages, laws and customs.

 

• The Censorship of the Press Act (1799) was passed by Wellesley during the fear of a French invasion, putting newspapers under official scrutiny.

 

• The Peshwa Baji Rao II accepted the Subsidiary Alliance through the Treaty of Bassein (1802), which led to the Second Anglo-Maratha War.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Wellesley was the elder brother of Arthur Wellesley, the later Duke of Wellington.

 

• The Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799) ended Tipu Sultan's rule.

 

• The Directors of the Company were unhappy with his costly policy and recalled him in 1805.

 

• Permanent Settlement was applied to Bengal, Bihar and Orissa and later to the Banaras division.

 

NOTE

 

• Establishment of Fort William College (Option 1): Fort William College was a genuine Wellesley initiative of 1800, intended to give the Company's servants a training in oriental languages, so it is associated with his tenure and is not the exception.

 

• Censorship of the Press Act of 1799 (Option 3): The Censorship of the Press Act was passed in 1799 under Wellesley in the context of Napoleonic fears, hence it belongs to his rule and cannot be the exception asked for in the question.

 

• Acceptance of the Subsidiary Alliance by the Peshwa (Option 4): The Peshwa's acceptance of the Subsidiary Alliance by the Treaty of Bassein in 1802 is a landmark of Wellesley's policy, therefore it is certainly associated with him and is not the odd one out.

question:
Consider the following statements about Lord Wellesley's policy.

1. The Nawab of Awadh was forced in 1801 to surrender more than half of his territory to the Company.

2. In 1803 the British captured Delhi and placed the Mughal emperor under their protection on a pension.

3. Mysore was the last state to accept the Subsidiary Alliance, in 1805.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: in 1801 Wellesley compelled Nawab Saadat Ali Khan of Awadh to cede nearly half of the state, including Rohilkhand and the lower Doab (अवध से 1801 में आधा क्षेत्र छीना गया)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: during the Second Anglo-Maratha War the British took Delhi in 1803, and Shah Alam II was placed under Company protection with a pension.

 

• Statement 3 is wrong because Mysore accepted the Subsidiary Alliance in 1799, after the fall of Tipu Sultan, when the Wodeyars were restored.

 

• The Bhonsle and Scindia were among the last major powers to enter it in 1803, after their defeat at Assaye and Argaon.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Peshwa signed the Treaty of Bassein on 31 December 1802.

 

• Arthur Wellesley won the Battle of Assaye (1803).

 

• The Nizam accepted the first Subsidiary Alliance in 1798 and increased the subsidiary force in 1800.

 

• The British Resident at the Mughal court exercised actual power in Delhi after 1803.

 

• The Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05) was fought after the Peshwa's alliance, and it ended with the Treaty of Surji-Anjangaon with Scindia.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 2): Choosing 1 and 3 only treats the Mysore date as 1805, but Mysore accepted subsidiary terms in 1799 after Tipu's fall, and the pair omits the true Delhi and pension event of 1803.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 3): Selecting 2 and 3 only ignores the Awadh cession of 1801, which was one of the harshest territorial exactions of Wellesley, and accepts a mistaken 1805 date for Mysore.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Accepting every statement is incorrect because Mysore had already accepted the system in 1799; no state is described correctly by the claim of a final 1805 entry in the third statement.

question: The Treaty of Amritsar (1809) was signed between the British East India Company and Maharaja Ranjit Singh during the Governor-Generalship of
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lord Minto I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Treaty of Amritsar (1809) was concluded under Lord Minto I (1807-13), with Charles Metcalfe as the British envoy (अमृतसर की संधि 1809 — मिंटो प्रथम और रणजीत सिंह)

 

• By it Ranjit Singh agreed to confine his rule to the north-west of the Sutlej, and the Company recognised his power in the Punjab north of that river.

 

• The treaty checked the Maharaja's ambition to unite the Sikh states of the Cis-Sutlej region and placed them under British protection.

 

• It was made in the context of fears of a Napoleonic advance towards India through Persia and Afghanistan.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Minto I also sent missions to Persia, Afghanistan and Sindh.

 

• Charles Metcalfe later became Governor-General (1835-36) and is called the Liberator of the Indian Press.

 

• Ranjit Singh went on to build the strong Sikh Empire with Lahore as capital.

 

• The Sutlej remained the frontier until the First Anglo-Sikh War of 1845-46.

 

NOTE

 

• Lord Cornwallis (Option 1): Lord Cornwallis served in 1786-93 and again briefly in 1805, long before Ranjit Singh had established his authority over the Punjab, so he had no dealings with the Maharaja.

 

• Lord Wellesley (Option 2): Lord Wellesley held office from 1798 to 1805, a period in which Ranjit Singh was a young chieftain consolidating power; the Amritsar settlement came four years after Wellesley left.

 

• Lord Amherst (Option 3): Lord Amherst served from 1823 to 1828 and is associated with the First Anglo-Burmese War of 1824-26, not with Ranjit Singh's agreement of 1809.

question: The Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817-18) under the Marquess of Hastings led to the abolition of the Peshwaship, and the last Peshwa, Baji Rao II, was exiled to
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bithur near Kanpur.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After defeat in the Third Anglo-Maratha War, also called the Pindari War, the Company abolished the office of Peshwa, and Baji Rao II was pensioned and exiled to Bithur (पेशवा पद का अंत — बाजीराव द्वितीय को बिठूर भेजा गया)

 

• Peshwa territories were annexed to the Bombay Presidency, and Pratap Singh was installed as a petty raja of Satara.

 

• The Pindaris, bands of mounted plunderers, were destroyed in the campaign, while Holkar was beaten at Mahidpur and Bhonsle at Sitabuldi.

 

• Bithur later became the residence of his adopted son Nana Sahib, a leader of the Revolt of 1857.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Marquess of Hastings (1813-23) also initiated the policy of paramountcy.

 

• He relaxed press restrictions by abolishing pre-censorship in 1818.

 

• The Ryotwari System of Thomas Munro was approved during his tenure.

 

• The Maratha confederacy ceased to be a political force after 1818.

 

• The Peshwa's pension of eight lakh rupees a year was paid to Baji Rao II at Bithur until his death in 1851.

 

NOTE

 

• Poona (Option 2): Poona (Pune) was the Peshwa's capital, which was occupied and where the Company set up its rule; Baji Rao was moved away from the capital to prevent any revival of Maratha intrigue there.

 

• Satara (Option 3): Satara became a small state under Chhatrapati Pratap Singh, a descendant of Shivaji, and not the place of the Peshwa's pension; it was annexed in 1848 under the Doctrine of Lapse.

 

• Nagpur (Option 4): Nagpur was the seat of the Bhonsle rulers and was annexed by Dalhousie in 1854; Baji Rao was not exiled there.

question:
Match the Governor-General in Column A with the measure/policy in Column B.

Column A: (a) Lord Wellesley (b) Lord Cornwallis (c) Lord Dalhousie (d) Marquess of Hastings

Column B: (i) Doctrine of Lapse (ii) Subsidiary Alliance (iii) Permanent Settlement (iv) Approval of the Ryotwari system in Madras
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Wellesley (a) is linked with (ii) Subsidiary Alliance, begun with the Nizam in 1798 (गवर्नर-जनरल और उनकी नीतियाँ — सही मिलान)

 

• Cornwallis (b) introduced (iii) the Permanent Settlement in 1793, fixing the land revenue of the zamindars for ever.

 

• Dalhousie (c) applied (i) the Doctrine of Lapse, annexing Satara in 1848 and Nagpur in 1854.

 

• Hastings (d) approved (iv) the Ryotwari System, introduced in the Madras Presidency by Thomas Munro.

 

• Wellesley's alliances began with Hyderabad in 1798, while Cornwallis's land arrangement of 1793 made the zamindars hereditary owners in Bengal, which fixes the second pairing.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Munro became Governor of Madras in 1820 and extended the ryotwari system there.

 

• The Mahalwari system was a third revenue arrangement introduced in 1833.

 

• Wellesley's scheme was a device of indirect rule in which the Company controlled the foreign relations of the state.

 

• The Doctrine of Lapse was dropped after the Revolt of 1857.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv (Option 1): This combination exchanges the policies of Wellesley and Cornwallis; the Permanent Settlement was introduced in 1793 by Cornwallis, whereas the Subsidiary Alliance belongs to Wellesley, so a-iii and b-ii cannot be right.

 

• a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii (Option 2): This combination makes Cornwallis the author of the Doctrine of Lapse, gives the Ryotwari approval to Dalhousie and the Permanent Settlement to Hastings; each of these three pairings is wrong, since lapse was Dalhousie's and permanent settlement was Cornwallis's.

 

• a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i (Option 4): This combination gives the ryotwari approval to Wellesley, the Subsidiary Alliance to Dalhousie and the Doctrine of Lapse to Hastings; only the Cornwallis pairing is right, and the other three pairings are all misplaced.

question: Who was the last Governor-General of Bengal and the first Governor-General of India under the Charter Act of 1833?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lord William Bentinck.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Lord William Bentinck (1828-35) became the first Governor-General of India when the Charter Act of 1833 converted the Bengal office into an all-India one (विलियम बेंटिक — भारत का प्रथम गवर्नर-जनरल)

 

• The Act vested all civil and military powers in the Governor-General-in-Council and ended the Company's trading functions.

 

• It also added a fourth ordinary Law Member to the council, the first being Thomas Babington Macaulay.

 

• Bentinck's tenure is best remembered for social and educational reforms and financial economy.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Bentinck had earlier been Governor of Madras, where the Vellore Mutiny (1806) cost him his post.

 

• The Charter Act of 1833 opened Company posts to all, irrespective of religion, race or birth, in principle.

 

• The Government of India Act 1858 later made the Governor-General the Viceroy.

 

• The first Viceroy was Lord Canning, who was also the last Governor-General.

 

NOTE

 

• Lord Amherst (Option 1): Lord Amherst (1823-28) preceded Bentinck as Governor-General of Bengal and presided over the First Anglo-Burmese War; he held only the Bengal post and never the all-India one.

 

• Lord Auckland (Option 2): Lord Auckland (1836-42) succeeded Bentinck and Metcalfe as Governor-General of India and is linked with the First Afghan War, so he was not the first holder of the title.

 

• Lord Ellenborough (Option 3): Lord Ellenborough (1842-44) followed Auckland and took action on the Afghan and Sindh questions; as a later holder he cannot have been the first Governor-General of India.

question:
Consider the following statements about the reforms of Lord William Bentinck.

1. The practice of Sati was declared illegal in 1829.

2. He launched a campaign to suppress thuggee.

3. English was made the medium of higher education following Macaulay's Minute and the resolution of 1835.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 2 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: Sati was prohibited in 1829 (Regulation XVII) with the support of Raja Ram Mohan Roy, first in Bengal and later in other presidencies (बेंटिक के सुधार — सती प्रथा निषेध 1829)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: Bentinck launched a vigorous campaign against thuggee, the organised highway murder and robbery by gangs, with William Sleeman leading the operation.

 

• Statement 3 is correct: Macaulay's Minute on education was accepted and the English Education Act of 1835 made English the language of official and higher instruction.

 

• All three belong to Bentinck's term, so all statements are valid.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Bentinck is regarded as the father of Western education in India because of his support for English education.

 

• Raja Ram Mohan Roy lobbied the Governor-General and later the Privy Council against any repeal of the Sati ban.

 

• Macaulay's Minute of 2 February 1835 attacked the orientalist approach and favoured English education.

 

• Bentinck also reduced the Army batta and cut expenditure to restore the Company's finances.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 2 only (Option 1): Opting for 1 and 2 only denies the education measure, yet the English Education Act and the acceptance of Macaulay's Minute in 1835 are listed among the achievements of Bentinck's term.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 3): Going with 2 and 3 only overlooks the abolition of Sati in 1829, which was the most celebrated social reform of Bentinck and the result of the efforts of Raja Ram Mohan Roy.

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 4): Choosing 1 and 3 only leaves out the suppression of thuggee, though Bentinck's campaign against the thugs, which was directed by William Sleeman, was among his principal acts.

question:
Arrange the following Governors-General in the chronological order of their tenure.

1. Lord Wellesley

2. Lord Cornwallis

3. William Bentinck

4. Marquess of Hastings
solution_text:
The correct answer is 2-1-4-3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Lord Cornwallis held office from 1786 to 1793, so he comes first of the four (गवर्नर-जनरलों का कालक्रम)

 

• Lord Wellesley followed in 1798-1805, with the Subsidiary Alliance and the Fourth Mysore War as his main events.

 

• The Marquess of Hastings governed in 1813-23 and was responsible for the Third Maratha War and the end of the Peshwaship.

 

• William Bentinck came last, in 1828-35, and he introduced the abolition of Sati and English education. The correct sequence is therefore Cornwallis, Wellesley, Hastings, Bentinck.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Between Wellesley and Hastings fell Minto I (1807-13), and between Hastings and Bentinck came Amherst (1823-28).

 

• Cornwallis returned for a second term in 1805 and died the same year.

 

• Charles Metcalfe served in 1835-36 after Bentinck, and Auckland followed in 1836.

 

• Bentinck, who had first been Governor-General of Bengal, became the Governor-General of India from 1833.

 

NOTE

 

• 1-2-4-3 (Option 1): This order places Wellesley ahead of Cornwallis, but Cornwallis held the post from 1786 while Wellesley arrived in 1798, so the opening pair is reversed even though the closing pair is right.

 

• 2-4-1-3 (Option 2): This order puts Hastings before Wellesley, which is impossible since Hastings (Marquess) served in 1813-23 after Wellesley's 1798-1805 tenure; the final position of Bentinck is correct.

 

• 2-1-3-4 (Option 3): This order places Bentinck ahead of Hastings, but Bentinck ruled from 1828, a full five years after Hastings had left in 1823, so the last two positions are exchanged.

question: Which Governor-General is known as the 'Liberator of the Indian Press' for removing restrictions on newspapers in 1835?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Charles Metcalfe.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sir Charles Metcalfe (acting Governor-General 1835-36) repealed the restrictive press regulations of 1823 and is hailed as the Liberator of the Indian Press (चार्ल्स मेटकाफ — भारतीय प्रेस के मुक्तिदाता)

 

• His Press Act of 1835 required only that the printer or publisher give details of the place of publication, abolishing licensing.

 

• The step led to a rapid growth of English and vernacular newspapers in the following years.

 

• Metcalfe served between Bentinck and Auckland, and earlier he negotiated the Treaty of Amritsar (1809) with Ranjit Singh.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The 1823 Licensing Regulations had been framed by John Adam during Amherst's period; Ram Mohan Roy protested against them.

 

• Lord Hastings had earlier abolished pre-censorship in 1818.

 

• Lytton's Vernacular Press Act (1878) re-imposed curbs, and Ripon repealed it in 1882.

 

• Wellesley's Censorship of the Press Act (1799) was the first major restriction.

 

NOTE

 

• William Bentinck (Option 1): William Bentinck is remembered for abolishing Sati and promoting English education; though he was liberal, the press law of 1835 was passed under his successor Metcalfe and carries the title.

 

• Lord Hastings (Option 2): Lord Hastings relaxed the press by abolishing censorship in 1818, a milder move that did not repeal the entire licensing system and for which he is not given the title of liberator.

 

• Lord Lytton (Option 4): Lord Lytton did the opposite and imposed the Vernacular Press Act of 1878 to curb criticism in Indian-language papers; he is associated with suppression and not with liberation.

question: The First Anglo-Afghan War (1839-42) occurred during the Governor-Generalship of
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lord Auckland.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Lord Auckland (1836-42) launched the First Anglo-Afghan War, sending an army to replace Dost Muhammad with Shah Shuja at Kabul (प्रथम अफगान युद्ध — लॉर्ड ऑकलैंड)

 

• The aim was to prevent Russian influence at Kabul and secure the north-western frontier of British India.

 

• The campaign ended in disaster in the winter of 1841-42, when the British garrison was destroyed during its retreat from Kabul.

 

• Auckland was succeeded by Ellenborough, who was sent to restore British prestige after the failure.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Second Afghan War (1878-80) took place under Lytton and ended with the Treaty of Gandamak.

 

• The Sikh Wars (1845-46, 1848-49) were fought under Hardinge and Dalhousie.

 

• Curzon later fixed relations with Afghanistan by Kabul Convention and created the North-West Frontier Province (1901).

 

• The Tripartite Treaty (1838) between the British, Ranjit Singh and Shah Shuja preceded the war.

 

NOTE

 

• Lord Lytton (Option 1): Lord Lytton (1876-80) fought the Second Anglo-Afghan War of 1878-80, not the First; the second war ended with the Treaty of Gandamak in 1879 and concerned the Forward Policy.

 

• Lord Dalhousie (Option 2): Lord Dalhousie (1848-56) won the Second Anglo-Sikh War and annexed Punjab in 1849, so his famous campaigns were in the Punjab and Burma and not in Afghanistan.

 

• Lord Curzon (Option 3): Lord Curzon (1899-1905) was a Viceroy, not a Governor-General, and his frontier policy included the North-West Frontier Province; Afghanistan was not at war with Britain at his time.

question: The Indian Slavery Act, which ended the legal status of slavery in India, was passed in 1843 under which Governor-General?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lord Ellenborough.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Lord Ellenborough (1842-44) presided over the abolition of the legal status of slavery in India (Act V of 1843) (भारत में दासता प्रथा का उन्मूलन — एलेनबरो, 1843)

 

• The Act prohibited courts and public officers from recognising or enforcing a claim of ownership over a person as a slave.

 

• Ellenborough is also remembered for the annexation of Sindh in 1843 after Charles Napier's victory at Miani.

 

• He succeeded Auckland and was recalled in 1844 by the Court of Directors.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Lord Hardinge I (1844-48) fought the First Anglo-Sikh War and signed the Treaty of Lahore in 1846.

 

• Dalhousie annexed Punjab in 1849.

 

• The Charter Act of 1833 had already directed the government to take steps to end slavery.

 

• The Act of 1843 was a legal abolition of the status, whereas the practice persisted in some regions.

 

NOTE

 

• Lord Hardinge I (Option 1): Lord Hardinge I governed from 1844 to 1848 and is better known for the First Anglo-Sikh War and the Treaty of Lahore of 1846 than for the slavery legislation, which had already been passed.

 

• Lord Dalhousie (Option 3): Lord Dalhousie took office in 1848, five years after the Act of 1843, and is known for annexation, railways and the telegraph, not for abolishing slavery.

 

• Lord Auckland (Option 4): Lord Auckland left India in 1842, the year before the Act of 1843 was passed, and was busy with the Afghan expedition that went badly.

question: Lord Dalhousie, who assumed charge as Governor-General in 1848, is noted for being the youngest Governor-General of India. He was how many years old at that time?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 36.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Lord Dalhousie took charge in 1848 at the age of 36, making him the youngest Governor-General of India (डलहौजी — 36 वर्ष की आयु में गवर्नर-जनरल)

 

• His term from 1848 to 1856 covered the Second Anglo-Sikh War, the annexation of Punjab (1849) and of Lower Burma after the Second Anglo-Burmese War (1852).

 

• He is regarded as the maker of modern India for the railways, telegraph and postal reforms.

 

• His annexations through the Doctrine of Lapse and the annexation of Awadh in 1856 created resentment before the Revolt of 1857.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Dalhousie was the son of the Earl of Dalhousie and had earlier been President of the Board of Trade in Britain.

 

• The Marquis title was conferred on him in 1849 for annexing Punjab.

 

• He left India in March 1856 and died in 1860.

 

• Canning succeeded him in 1856.

 

• Dalhousie also presented the famous railway minute of 1853 and set up the Public Works Department as a separate department.

 

NOTE

 

• 32 (Option 1): The age of 32 is too low; Dalhousie, born in April 1812, was already 35 when he landed in India in early 1848 and turned 36 soon after, which makes him youngest but not 32.

 

• 40 (Option 2): The age of 40 is not correct for Dalhousie in 1848; he was born in 1812, so he was about 36, and a forty-year-old would have been born in 1808, which does not fit.

 

• 44 (Option 4): The age of 44 is far above his actual age; Dalhousie was the youngest Governor-General at his appointment, and being 44 would have placed him among the ordinary older appointees.

question: The Doctrine of Lapse was first applied by Lord Dalhousie to which princely state in 1848?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Satara.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The first annexation under the Doctrine of Lapse was Satara in 1848, when the ruler died without a natural heir and his adoption was disallowed (व्यपगत का सिद्धांत — पहला शिकार सतारा, 1848)

 

• The doctrine held that a dependent ruler could not adopt an heir without the Company's sanction; in the absence of a natural heir the state 'lapsed' to the paramount power.

 

• Later victims included Sambalpur (1849), Jaitpur, Baghat, Udaipur, Jhansi and Nagpur (1854).

 

• The doctrine was withdrawn after the Revolt of 1857, as stated in Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Dalhousie also abolished the titles and pensions of Nawab of Carnatic, Tanjore and Peshwa's heir Nana Sahib.

 

• Awadh was annexed in 1856 on the ground of misgovernment.

 

• The Doctrine was not applied to Punjab, which was annexed after the Second Sikh War in 1849.

 

• Dalhousie's policy left the heirs of Jhansi and Nagpur without succession.

 

NOTE

 

• Jhansi (Option 1): Jhansi was taken under the Doctrine of Lapse only after the death of Raja Gangadhar Rao in the early 1850s, so it was a later victim and not the first state affected.

 

• Nagpur (Option 3): Nagpur was annexed in 1854 after the death of Raghuji III without a legal heir; the date is clear and it follows Satara by six years, so it was not the first lapse.

 

• Awadh (Option 4): Awadh was annexed in 1856 on the pretext of misgovernment and not under the Doctrine of Lapse, because the Nawab had no problem of an adopted heir at that stage.
